# Diagnosing Flickering in a 24V DC-DC Converter System

When two high-current flashing lights cause the entire body of a 24V truck to flicker, the issue is almost certainly insufficient current capacity on the return path or a ground loop interaction between the high-frequency switching and sensitive loads. Based on the wiring description providedâwhere the supply uses 12 AWG but each load drops to 18 AWG after a distribution blockâthe system is susceptible to voltage drops that manifest as visible flickering when the load profile changes rapidly.

### The Impact of Flasher Frequency on Voltage Drop

Flashing units typically operate by rapidly switching current on and off, often at frequencies between 1 to 2 Hz for standard warning lights or higher for strobes. While the human eye averages this into a stable "on" state when the lights are off, the moment they activate, the DC-DC converter must supply the peak current almost instantly.

The core issue here is likely the impedance of the return path. You mentioned using 18 AWG cables from the distribution block to each load. While acceptable for steady-state lighting loads (perhaps 3Aâ5A per bulb), these cables have a significant voltage drop at high currents. When the flasher unit engages, it draws a surge current that can momentarily exceed the continuous rating of the DC-DC converter or the capacity of the distribution block's connections.

If the ground return path has even a few milliohms of resistance, a 20A surge (which is plausible for incandescent bulbs during startup) across 18 AWG wire can drop several volts before reaching the bulbs. The DC-DC converter might interpret this voltage sag as a need to boost output, or simply fail to maintain regulation, causing the perceived flicker on adjacent lights that share the same ground rail.

### Analyzing the Distribution Block and Grounding Strategy

The distribution block acts as a single point of failure in your topology. When you connect multiple loads to one block, you are forcing all return currents to converge at that specific node before returning to the DC-DC converter's ground terminal. If the flasher unit shares this ground rail with the body lights, the high-frequency switching noise or the transient current spikes from the flasher will couple directly into the voltage rails of the other lights.

This is a classic ground bounce problem. The solution is not necessarily to change the DC-DC converter, but to isolate the return paths. Ideally, each lighting circuit should have its own dedicated ground wire running directly back to the main battery negative or a common chassis ground point near the DC-DC converter, rather than relying solely on the distribution block as the primary return junction.

### Implementation: Isolating Flasher Loads

To resolve this while keeping the system as original as possible, consider rewiring the return path for the flashing lights exclusively. Instead of daisy-chaining through the distribution block's main ground lug, run a dedicated 12 AWG or thicker ground wire from the flasher unit directly to the chassis near the DC-DC converter.

If you must keep the existing wiring layout, ensure that the distribution block has sufficient terminal capacity. Many small distribution blocks have thin internal busbars that cannot handle the combined surge of all connected loads plus the flasher unit. Upgrading the distribution block to one with thicker copper busbars or using a heavy-gauge main ground strap (12 AWG) from the block to the battery/chassis can eliminate the bottleneck.

### Considering LED Replacement as a Mitigation Strategy

You mentioned considering an LED replacement. This is a highly effective mitigation strategy because LEDs draw significantly less current than incandescent bulbs and have a much faster, more linear turn-on time, reducing the inrush surge that causes voltage drops. However, if you proceed with LEDs, ensure they are compatible with 24V systems and include built-in resistors or constant-current drivers to prevent them from drawing excessive current when paired with standard flasher units designed for high-resistance incandescent loads.

Some modern LED flashers are specifically designed to work with low-wattage LED arrays, but mixing a traditional high-inductance flasher unit with a low-load LED circuit can sometimes cause the flasher to malfunction or fail to flash correctly. If you switch to LEDs, verify that the existing flasher unit is rated for the reduced load, or consider upgrading to an electronic flasher module designed for LED compatibility.

### Final Verification Steps

Before finalizing any changes, use a multimeter to measure the voltage at the distribution block and at the load terminals while the flashing lights are active. If you see a voltage drop greater than 0.5V during the "on" phase of the flasher, your wiring gauge or connection points are the culprit. Tighten all connections at the DC-DC converter output and the main battery negative terminal; corrosion or loose lugs in these areas often exacerbate flickering issues that appear to be wiring problems.
